title: When the Cellar Sings
premise: Folklorist Mirabel Quintana has spent three years in the village of Hollowmere recording songs no one will sing twice, telling themselves the cellar noises beneath their rented cottage are pipes, settling stone, anything. When the church bell — melted down in 1911 — rings across the frost, the village's oldest families begin counting aloud at night, and Mirabel realizes the songs they collected are a ledger: every verse sung is a name the cellar remembers. The count must reach one hundred before the frost finishes its final windowpane pattern, and the last name on it belongs to Mirabel's found family, the Ashcombes. To save them, Mirabel must sing the songs back to the cellar in reverse, trading their own belonging in Hollowmere for the truth they spent three years refusing to hear.
about_author: Rosalind Halloran is the pen name of a former archivist who spent a decade cataloguing hymnals and folk song collections in rural parish libraries before turning to fiction. They write horror about the things communities agree not to mention, and live somewhere with very deep cellars.

chapters.title: The Bell That Wasn't Cast
chapters.summary: Mirabel's POV. On the first hard frost, the melted bell rings at midnight, and every villager pretends not to hear it. Mirabel reviews three years of field recordings and finds verses spliced into songs that no informant remembers singing. The emotional beat is creeping self-doubt: the rational explanations Mirabel built are beginning to sound like someone else's voice rehearsing them.

chapters.title: Counting the Ashcombes
chapters.summary: Alternating between Mirabel and young Wren Ashcombe. The family that took Mirabel in begins sleepwalking to the churchyard, counting aloud in a dialect dead since 1911; Wren reaches forty-one before waking, terrified. Mirabel discovers each recorded song shortens the count's distance. The beat is loyalty straining against dread as Mirabel hides what they know to keep the family calm.

chapters.title: What the Ledger Wants Sung
chapters.summary: Mirabel's POV, deepening into horror. In the parish archive Mirabel finds the 1911 bell was recast from a singing stone, and the village elders have been feeding names to the cellar for generations to buy their own safety. Confronted, the elders offer Mirabel a place on the safe side of the ledger if they surrender the Ashcombes' names. The beat is power's corruption made intimate: belonging offered at exactly the price of truth.

chapters.title: Sung Backwards
chapters.summary: Mirabel's POV, climax and resolution. On the final frost night, with the count at ninety-nine, Mirabel plays every recording in reverse into the cellar mouth, giving back the songs and their own name with them. The Ashcombes wake; the bell cracks mid-peal; the frost pattern stops one pane short of finished. Mirabel leaves Hollowmere alive but unremembered by it — belonging traded away, truth kept, the recordings blank.
